title: In Texas, the GOP’s Last Urban Stronghold Swings Blue
author: Michael Barajas
content:
The blue wave that helped Texas Democrats win their first statewide offices in
more than three decades is also set to reshape policy in Republicans’ last
urban stronghold in the state.

In Tarrant County, home to Fort Worth, Democrat Alisa Simmons decisively beat
incumbent GOP county executive Tim O’Hare—a MAGA acolyte who, during his
single term in countywide office, helped [fan baseless
claims](https://boltsmag.org/tarrant-county-election-fraud-task-force/) of
widespread voter fraud and who [fought to suppress community
outrage](https://boltsmag.org/jail-crisis-looms-over-tarrant-county-sheriff-
election/) over local jail deaths and voting restrictions. Simmons’ win
Tuesday night is part of a larger shift to the left in Fort Worth that will
usher in a new Democratic majority on the county’s five-member governing board
and a new Democratic district attorney.

Simmons last year became a prime target for the Republicans who have long
dominated Tarrant County government, when the GOP majority on the county board
gerrymandered the local electoral maps to favor their party’s candidates and
push her out of office—prompting Simmons to run for countywide office this
year instead of seeking reelection in her newly redrawn district.

Celebrating her win and that of other local Democratic candidates who helped
flip Tarrant County’s government on Tuesday night, Simmons [told
supporters](https://www.facebook.com/CommALSimmons/videos/1545688480924103/),
“You can expect us to manage this county with heart, compassion, personal
responsibility, justice and ethics.”

Simmons has been one of the loudest champions of local advocates for criminal
justice reform since being elected to Tarrant County’s governing board, called
the commissioners court, in 2022—from organizing press conferences with
families grieving the loss of loved ones at the county’s notoriously deadly
jail, to hosting county forums to discuss jail conditions and clashing with
the local GOP sheriff during county board meetings.

Pamela Young, executive director of United Fort Worth and a longtime organizer
for criminal justice reform in North Texas, told _Bolts_ that she’s hoping for
Simmons to rally for criminal justice reforms as county executive. “Our
current county judge and the majority on that court, they haven’t been doing
their job—they’ve been erecting Ten Commandments statues, they’ve been
enacting draconian rules in the courtroom, and throwing people out for calling
them racist.”

Jail oversight and ballot access have become flashpoints for Tarrant County
politics in recent years, in part because of Simmons’ pushback on the county
board. While she advocated for people who lost loved ones at the county jail,
O’Hare, her opponent on Tuesday, had [grieving
family](https://boltsmag.org/jail-crisis-looms-over-tarrant-county-sheriff-
election/) members and [local
organizers](https://www.wfaa.com/article/news/local/tarrant-county/residents-
booted-tarrant-county-commissioners-
court/287-5e866924-9c0c-452c-b5f2-4b6677317951) removed from county hearings
for confronting the board over deadly local jail conditions.

O’Hare also drew community pushback earlier this year for championing a plan
to dramatically reduce the number of county polling places during the midterm
elections. As citizens crowded county hearings to decry the plan, O’Hare
pushed to curtail critical public testimony and even had citizens removed and
arrested for pushing back against the plan—including a [former
lawmaker](https://www.texastribune.org/2026/08/05/texas-lon-burnam-arrest-
jail-tarrant-county-voting/) who represented Fort Worth in the state
legislature for nearly two decades and local activists like EJ Carrion.

Carrion, who is [still facing misdemeanor
charges](https://www.kera.org/2026/09/17/fort-worth-activist-arrested-for-
cursing-at-tarrant-county-commissioners-meeting-gets-case-delayed/) for
speaking out earlier this year at a county hearing to axe polling places, says
Simmons’ win marks a sea change for Tarrant County. “Alisa Simmons winning is
more valuable to Tarrant County than James Talarico,” he told _Bolts_.
“Tarrant County has been the epicenter of extremism, but now it’s becoming the
epicenter of change.”

Simmons’ win in Tarrant County is also particularly meaningful for organizers
in Texas who have fought for jail reforms in recent years. [As _Bolts_ has
previously reported](https://boltsmag.org/tarrant-county-jail-deaths-2026/),
Simmons has pushed back for years against Bill Waybourn, the local Republican
sheriff who has seen jail deaths increase on his watch. Krishaveni Gundu, the
co-founder and executive director of the Texas Jail Project, who had been
closely watching Simmons’ race, says her win represents “a significant and
exciting victory for transparency and accountability” over jail deaths in the
state.

Waybourn’s management of jail death was also aided by another local Republican
ally, DA Phil Sorrels, who wrote a letter to the state attorney general
arguing for limiting investigations into some deaths of people under custody.

Sorrels lost his reelection race Tuesday to Democrat Tiffany Burks, who
[campaigned](https://www.mobilize.us/hillcountydems/event/1028484/) alongside
Simmons, adding to the shake-up in local government.

“Under Simmons' leadership, we look forward to the commissioners’ court
holding the sheriff's office and county jail more accountable,” Gundu told
_Bolts_. “We are hopeful that she will succeed in translating the voters'
mandate into meaningful, substantive change.”

  
_The story has been updated on Wednesday to reflect the final results in the
elections for county commissioner_.
